plan.topic: Tirzepatide and a faster resting heart rate: what the label reports and when a racing heart means calling
plan.angle: 08:00 body-worry Short, tight arm. Sentence 1, 14 words or fewer: 'Resting heart rate up since starting tirzepatide? The label reports that.' By 6 s, the one new fact: the label's average heart-rate increase and how often a fast heartbeat was reported vs placebo, copied exactly from the Zepbound PI (rev. 28 Aug 2026) with the trial population named. If the label gives only wording, use its qualitative wording. Leave out the wearable cohort, which is observational. Untagged line: tell your prescriber if your watch shows a steady rise. When to get help: a racing heartbeat at rest that doesn't settle, chest pain, fainting or shortness of breath means your local urgent care or emergency number. Then the scoped don't-stop line, the Exp F line second to last, 'Not personal advice', the prescriber line and the closing line. Calm, neutral mascot on the risk lines, and no heart-damage imagery.
plan.why: A felt symptom wearable users notice, with low competition and no InforMed coverage. It's a calm 'is this normal?' format with tirzepatide in the title, our best-performing Short format.

package.title: Tirzepatide: Is a Faster Resting Heart Rate Normal? #shorts
package.description:
Tirzepatide's placebo-controlled trials in adults with type 2 diabetes showed an average heart-rate rise of 2–4 beats a minute, vs 1 on placebo. That's an average, not a prediction.
A racing heartbeat at rest that doesn't settle, chest pain, fainting or shortness of breath means calling your local emergency number or urgent care right away.
For anything that isn't one of those emergency signs, don't stop or change your medicine on your own.
Source: Mounjaro Prescribing Information, section 6.1 (revised 08/2026): https://uspl.lilly.com/mounjaro/mounjaro.html
#Tirzepatide #GLP1 #Type2Diabetes
Not personal advice. Talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether it's right for you.

factcheck.summary: I checked the one factual claim against the live Mounjaro Prescribing Information (revised 8/2026), and it is correct. Section 6.1 says Mounjaro "resulted in a mean increase in heart rate of 2 to 4 beats per minute", compared with 1 beat per minute on placebo. The pooled placebo-controlled trials in that label are in adults with type 2 diabetes, and scene s2 names that population correctly. The framing is accurate: it is called an average, not a prediction. The checking tip and when-to-call steps carry no source tag, which is right. The safety lines are in the required order: the scoped don't-stop line, then "Not personal advice", then the prescriber line. The Exp F line and closing line come at the end. By my count there are about 156 spoken words, inside the standard 135–160 arm. The hook and title pay off. There are two small wording issues, both optional.

issues.claim: Tirzepatide: +2–4 bpm on average vs +1 on placebo
issues.problem: With the sound off, the opening card doesn't name the population (type 2 diabetes trials), and the placebo number has no unit. The population first appears on the s2 stat card.
issues.fix: Tirzepatide (T2D trials): +2–4 bpm on average vs +1 bpm on placebo

issues.claim: chest pain, fainting or shortness of breath means calling your local urgent care or emergency number right away
issues.problem: This follows the house wording, but someone with chest pain or fainting should be pointed to the emergency number first, not urgent care. It's optional polish, not inaccurate.
issues.fix: A racing heartbeat at rest that doesn't settle, chest pain, fainting or shortness of breath means calling your local emergency number or urgent care right away.
